item.title: FX option expiries for 27 October 10am New York cut
item.description:
There are a couple of key expiry levels to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below.

The first is for EUR/USD at the 1.1175 level, with the strike holding roughly within 10 pips of the spot price. That could help keep price action more contained around current levels, particularly with markets awaiting major central bank decisions later this week. Having said that, the technical downside momentum looks to be taking over again for EUR/USD and that could open up a push towards testing the month's lows around 1.1111 in the bigger picture.

Then, there is a sizable cluster of expiries for USD/JPY layered between 157.75 to 158.00. All three are sitting just above the current spot price, so they could exert some magnetic pull on price action and potentially keep the pair more anchored around the region ahead of the cut later. However, just be wary that any fresh intervention warnings from Japanese officials could easily override that influence.

And lastly, there is one for AUD/USD at the 0.7030 level - just a little over 10 pips away from the spot price. That could also act as a potential magnet for price action, with the expiry level tying closely with the 100-day moving average at 0.7031 currently. Put together, that could act as a bit of a resistance point for AUD/USD in the session ahead should trading conditions remain relatively subdued.

In the bigger picture, the pair will still be largely influenced by broader risk sentiment and dollar flows before we get to the key central bank decisions and big tech earnings later this week. Besides that, the Australia CPI data tomorrow will also be one to note for the aussie as that could have the potential to induce more volatility to the pair.

But for now though, it's all a waiting game as traders will likely be content to stick with a more patient and cautious tone before we get into the bigger events on the week.

item.title: Japan finance minister Katayama warns of decisive action as yen intervention risks linger
item.description:
Japan finance minister Katayama is out with another warning to markets today, reaffirming that Tokyo remains ready to step in if necessary to defend the yen. Her comments:

  • Government stands ready to take decisive action in the FX market
  • Always watching market moves with a high sense of urgency, including at this very moment
  • Must ensure yen movements reflect economic fundamentals
  • Hopes to maintain market trust in the yen and the Takaichi administration's fiscal policy through transparent, consistent communication

Her remarks are not anything that we haven't heard of before. But as always, it is best for traders to take note on the tone and frequency of the communication.

The comments above certainly underscore a more firm language, particularly the reference to taking "decisive action". Then again, it is a phrase that Tokyo officials have used in the past in associating with the threat of direct currency intervention.

Having said that, I wouldn't read too much into the remarks as suggesting that intervention is imminent. As mentioned above, Katayama has used similarly forceful language before.

So if anything else, this feels like Tokyo attempting to keep the pressure on yen sellers rather than signalling an immediate move.

For now, USD/JPY is seeing a modest rebound after the sharp drop on Thursday last week. The pair is trading back above the 157 mark and is starting to take another look at key resistance in the form of the 200-day moving average at around 158.51. The psychologically important 160 level is still a little far away but it isn't completely out of the picture yet. So, that should continue to keep intervention risks on the radar - especially if we start seeing another rapid and one-sided depreciation in the yen.

At least for the time being, I reckon Tokyo is still hoping that verbal intervention will do enough to keep speculative pressures in check. With the BOJ decision coming up later this week, policymakers would also surely prefer to see how markets react to that before considering more direct action.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bond market tensions ease but Treasury yields near 5% and France's debt risks keep investors on edge
item.description:
There is a bit of a welcome relief in global bonds to start the new week, particularly in Europe after Moody's affirmed France's Aa3 credit rating. Meanwhile, Treasury yields have also settled down a fair bit after an extremely volatile period earlier this month. But in looking at where things are right now, there is still plenty of tension lurking beneath the surface.

For one, 10-year Treasury yields are still sitting just below the 5% mark for the time being. And over in Europe, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread remains at levels that would have surely been alarming just a few months ago.

So while the selling pressure in the bond market has eased for now, the underlying concerns haven't really changed all that much. And as much as that offers some breathing room for broader markets, there are still plenty of reasons to be cautious.

The Fed decision tomorrow is one obvious catalyst, even if policymakers are widely expected to leave interst rates unchanged. And beyond that, I'm also keeping a close watch on big tech earnings this week.

On the latter, there's a growing concern over whether the enormous spending behind the AI boom can actually justify the returns. And if earnings from the likes of Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all back that sentiment, we could see a rather nasty bout of volatility kick in again. That will especially be the case if investors start seeking safety in government bonds again while becoming more wary of riskier corporate debt. If so, falling Treasury yields might not necessarily be the good news that stock markets are hoping for.

Looking to 10-year Treasury yields, the 5% mark remains the key level to watch. A firmer break below the 4.92% region could open up a further retracement towards the 100-day moving average (red line) around 4.77% next. Otherwise, a move back above 5% would keep the recent consolidation in focus with the October highs around 5.30% still in the picture.

Over in Europe, Moody's decision to reaffirm France's Aa3 credit rating at the end of last week has certainly helped to ease some nerves.

French bond yields have come off the boil, with the France-Germany 10-year yield spread now retreating towards 153 bps after racing to its highest levels since 2011 last week.

However, let's not forget that Moody's also retained a negative outlook on France. The country's fiscal problems haven't suddenly disappeared overnight, nor has the political uncertainty surrounding efforts to bring its budget deficit under control. Those issues are still very much in the picture as we get into the new week.

In any case, the chart above says plenty about how fragile the situation remains. The spread is still holding above the key 150 bps threshold, leaving the door open for another push higher if fiscal concerns return to the spotlight.

For now, markets may be enjoying a bit of calm. But with major central bank decisions, big tech earnings and France's fiscal troubles all still in play, I wouldn't mistake that for a clean bill of health. No pun intended. ;)

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European markets face a quiet calendar today as central banks and big tech earnings loom
item.description:
European traders will be greeted with a rather bare economic calendar when they get to their desks today, and I reckon that might suit some market players just fine considering what is on the agenda later this week.

In terms of data releases, we only have French consumer confidence for October and the ECB's survey on euro area lending for September. Otherwise, markets will largely be left to their own devices as traders wait on the central bank bonanza to roll into town.

Wall Street at least provided a more positive lead in overnight trading, with the S&P 500 posting 0.7% gains and the Nasdaq closing 0.8% higher. Tech stocks helped to drive the rebound but caution is very much still up in the air, especially with the recent volatility surrounding the AI trade.

As for geopolitical tensions, we are seeing more of the same old, same old. Fresh diplomatic efforts involving Iran are offering some hope of de-escalation but continued attacks on Saudi Arabia are keeping oil supply risks firmly in the picture.

As such, I wouldn't be surprised if we see traders take on a more reserved and cautious approach to trading today. After all, the focus now turns to the BOC and Fed decisions tomorrow, followed by the ECB on Thursday and BOJ on Friday. And that is without mentioning big tech earnings with Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all set to put the AI spending debate back under the spotlight.

For today, I would look to bond yields, oil prices and the broader risk mood for clues on what might drive trading sentiment before we get to the bigger events this week. But without any major economic catalyst to latch on to, any notable moves may have more to do with positioning flows ahead of those events rather than any genuine market conviction I would say.

item.title: Ethereum Foundation “dump” is a $6.4m treasury sale, not a crisis
item.description:
A sale of this size has no meaningful effect on ETH supply or price, coming in at well under 0.1% of daily trading volume. The more relevant support for ETH is around $2,300, where it has been trading, and the broader flow picture: buying from Bitmine is fading, and spot ETF flows matter more than one-off Foundation conversions. A series of larger Foundation sales into weakness would be the scenario that turns this into a genuine supply story.

--- Crypto Twitter called it a dump, but the Ethereum Foundation selling $6.4 million of ETH to cover its running costs is a budget line, not a bear signal.

Summary:

  • The Ethereum Foundation sold around 2,785 ETH, worth about $6.4 million, for the USDS stablecoin on CoW Swap
  • Social media posts framed the sale as the Foundation dumping ETH
  • The sale equals well under 0.1% of a single day’s ETH trading volume, and less than Bitmine bought last week
  • The Foundation’s treasury policy sets out regular ETH sales to fund operations when cash reserves fall below about 2.5 years of costs
  • It cut its 2026 budget by around 40% and stakes about 70,000 ETH to reduce reliance on sales

The Ethereum Foundation sold around 2,785 ETH, worth roughly $6.4 million, according to on-chain tracker Onchain Lens, swapping the tokens for USDS, the dollar stablecoin issued by the Sky ecosystem, through the decentralised exchange CoW Swap. Within minutes, crypto Twitter had turned a routine treasury transaction into the Foundation “dumping” ETH. I have read some overblown crypto headlines in my time, but this one deserves a closer look, because the gap between the noise and what actually happened is a useful lesson for anyone trying to trade off on-chain alerts.

Start with the size. Around $6.4 million sounds like a lot until you set it against a market that traded more than $8 billion of ETH in the same 24 hours. The sale was well under a tenth of one percent of a single day’s volume. Bitmine, the largest corporate ETH holder, bought nearly four times as much ETH last week alone.The same day, trackers flagged another “sell” alert: a wallet that bought around 100,000 ETH at about $0.31 in Ethereum’s 2014 token sale moved roughly 1,500 ETH, worth about $3.5 million, to exchanges over eight hours. Early holders taking profit after a gain of several thousand times is not news either. Combined, the two moves still amount to well under 0.2% of a day’s trading.

Then consider why the Foundation sells at all. It is a non-profit that pays developers, researchers and grants, and it cannot pay salaries in ETH. Its treasury policy, published in June 2025, says plainly that it converts ETH into cash on a regular schedule, through exchanges or on-chain swaps, when its reserves drop below roughly two and a half years of operating costs. Swapping into a dollar stablecoin on a public exchange is that policy in action, not a secret exit.

If anything, the Foundation is trying to sell less, not more. It announced a cut of around 40% to its 2026 budget in June and is shifting towards an endowment model, while it began staking about 70,000 ETH in February to earn rewards without selling the tokens themselves. Earlier this year it also sold 10,000 ETH directly to Bitmine in a private deal, which kept the coins off the open market altogether.

None of this means Foundation sales never matter. A steady run of larger sales, especially into a falling market, would add real supply. One $6 million swap does not.

What to watch next: whether further sales follow from the same Foundation address in the coming weeks, which would point to a bigger quarterly conversion rather than a one-off; the Foundation’s own transparency reports, which should explain its cash needs; and ETH’s response around the $2,300 area, where it has been trading. If ETH holds up through any further sales, that confirms the market sees them for what they are. The practical lesson is simple: before reacting to a “dump” alert, check the size against daily volume and whether the seller has a published reason to sell.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: South Korea Q3 GDP grows 1.0%, beating forecasts as AI chip boom lifts exports
item.description:
The strength of the beat, and the KOSPI sidecar on a sharp rally, underline how heavily Korean assets now trade on the AI chip cycle. That cuts both ways: it supports exporters and chip names while global AI demand holds up, but leaves the market exposed to any wobble in the global AI trade. The data reinforce the Bank of Korea’s hawkish bias after its July and September hikes, which should support the won and keep pressure on short-end bond yields. Weak consumption is the main argument against further tightening, so household-sensitive sectors are likely to keep lagging.

---

South Korea is riding the AI chip boom hard enough to set off market circuit-breakers, but its households are sitting this one out.

Summary:

  • South Korea’s Q3 GDP grew 1.0% q/q, beating the 0.7% forecast and up from 0.6% in Q2; y/y growth was 3.4% versus 3.0% expected
  • The Bank of Korea estimates semiconductors drive about half of growth; annual growth could reach 3.7% if Q4 holds at Q3 levels
  • Exports rose 2.3% and facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by chip equipment
  • Private consumption fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years, hit by a stock slump and auto strikes
  • Exports topped $800 billion in January to September and are on track to pass $1 trillion this year
  • The KOSPI’s strong rise triggered a sidecar halt on program trading

South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as the global AI chip boom lifted exports and investment, advance Bank of Korea estimates showed on Tuesday, though weak household spending marked a notable soft spot. Gross domestic product rose 1.0% from the previous quarter, beating the 0.7% median forecast in a Reuters poll and accelerating from 0.6% in the second quarter.

Korean equities rallied strongly on the session, with the move in the KOSPI triggering a sidecar, a temporary halt on program trading that the Korea Exchange applies when index futures move sharply, to cool momentum-driven orders.

The scale of the beat was striking against the central bank’s own expectations. The Bank of Korea had forecast 0.3% growth for the quarter in August, when it projected 3.3% growth for the year. If fourth-quarter output simply holds at third-quarter levels, annual growth would now come in at around 3.7%. A central bank official estimated that semiconductors are driving about half of the economy’s growth.

Exports rose 2.3% in the quarter on demand for chips, machinery and electrical equipment, while facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by semiconductor manufacturing equipment. South Korea’s exports topped $800 billion in the first nine months, already above last year’s full-year record, putting the country on track to become only the fourth to pass $1 trillion in a year, after the US, China and Germany.

The weak link is consumption. Private spending fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years, as financial services activity dropped amid a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers. The central bank expects a gradual recovery as chip firms’ dividend payouts in the fourth quarter and employee bonuses early next year lift household incomes, though one economist cautioned that a soft labour market and restrictive interest rates limit the scope for a strong rebound. Consumer sentiment also slipped in October.

The Bank of Korea held rates last week after back-to-back hikes in July and September but kept a hawkish stance, and today’s data give it little reason to soften that. On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4%, also above the 3.0% expected. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China September industrial profits jump 14.4% y/y, rebounding from 4.2% in August
item.description:
The rebound offers a modest positive surprise for Chinese assets at a time when sentiment is fragile, with onshore equities in a bear market and Morgan Stanley warning of further downside in offshore shares. Industrial and materials stocks are the most direct beneficiaries, and the data may slightly ease concerns about a sharp earnings slowdown. Commodity-linked currencies such as the Australian dollar could find mild support from any read-through to Chinese industrial demand. That said, the gently slowing year-to-date trend and the lack of a sector breakdown limit how far markets are likely to run with the headline.

  • PBOC sets USD/ CNY central rate at 6.7171 (vs. estimate at 6.6731)

China’s factory profits shook off August’s slump in style, though the year-to-date trend is still drifting gently lower beneath the bounce.

Summary:

  • China’s industrial profits rose 14.4% y/y in September, up from 4.2% in August
  • Year-to-date profits rose 15.5% in January to September, down slightly from 15.7% in January to August
  • August’s 4.2% was the slowest single-month growth since November 2025
  • In January to August, mining and manufacturing led gains while utilities declined
  • High-tech and AI-related manufacturing have been strong performers this year
  • September’s rise comes on top of a strong base, after profits jumped more than 21% in September last year

Profits at China’s industrial firms rose 14.4% year on year in September, a sharp rebound from 4.2% growth in August, official data showed on Tuesday. Cumulative profits for the first nine months of the year rose 15.5%, edging down from 15.7% in the January to August period.

The September reading marks a strong recovery after August’s weak result, which was the slowest single-month growth since November 2025 and had followed an 11.2% rise in July. The rebound suggests August’s slowdown was not the start of a sustained downturn in corporate earnings, although year-to-date growth has continued to drift lower, from 17.6% in the January to July period to 15.5% now.

Industrial profits data, published monthly by the National Bureau of Statistics, cover larger industrial companies across mining, manufacturing and utilities. The figures are watched as a gauge of corporate health and pricing power in the world’s second-largest economy, and of firms’ capacity to invest and hire. Monthly readings can be volatile, so the year-to-date figure is often a better guide to the underlying trend.

Breakdowns for September were not available at the time of writing. In the January to August period, growth was led by mining, where profits rose about 35%, and manufacturing, up about 17%, while utilities recorded a decline of around 12%. High-tech and AI-related manufacturing had been strong performers, with computers and communications equipment profits more than doubling, though subdued domestic demand weighed on profitability in some industries.

The rebound comes against a difficult backdrop for Chinese markets. Onshore equities are in a bear market, and Morgan Stanley warned this week that offshore Chinese shares could fall a further 10% to 15% before reaching a valuation floor, citing a weakening economy among other pressures. Firmer industrial earnings offer some counterweight to that gloomy view, at least for the industrial sector.

The details of the September release, particularly which sectors drove the rebound and whether domestic demand is improving, will determine whether the strength proves durable or whether it partly reflects the month-to-month volatility typical of this series. The rise is all the more notable because it comes on top of a strong September last year, when profits jumped more than 21%. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan services PPI picks up to 3.7% as August revised lower, backing BoJ hike path
item.description:
The downward revision to August makes the September print more hawkish than the headline suggests: services prices are accelerating, not just holding. That adds weight to the case for the BoJ’s Outlook Report to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached 2%, and supports December hike pricing, lending the yen modest support into Friday. Short-end JGB yields could edge higher as markets price a firmer BoJ tone. Oil-driven cost pressure from the Iran conflict remains a background inflation risk, but this data shows domestic, labour-driven pressure building too. The vote split and Ueda’s press conference remain the bigger yen catalysts.

---

Earlier:

  • Japan September services PPI holds at 3.7% y/y, in line with forecast, before BoJ

--- A quiet downward revision to August turned Japan’s in-line services print into an acceleration, and that’s the version of the story the BoJ will be reading this week.

Summary:

  • Japan’s services producer price index rose 3.7% y/y in September, matching expectations
  • August was revised down to 3.5% from 3.7%, so September marks an acceleration
  • The BoJ watches the index for how far firms are passing rising labour costs on to service prices
  • Goods producer price inflation slowed to 6.8% in September from 7.6%
  • The BoJ is expected to hold at 1.25% when its two-day meeting ends Friday, while signalling readiness for further hikes
  • Focus is on whether the Outlook Report effectively declares underlying inflation has reached 2%

Japan’s services producer price index rose 3.7% year on year in September, in line with expectations and faster than a downwardly revised 3.5% gain in August, Bank of Japan data showed on Tuesday. The pick-up points to mounting service-sector price pressure ahead of a BoJ meeting this week that is expected to leave rates on hold while signalling further tightening ahead.

The revision changes the picture. August’s reading was initially reported at 3.7%, which had suggested September would merely match the prior month. With August now at 3.5%, the September figure marks an acceleration rather than a steady pace, a more hawkish read for policymakers watching whether inflation is becoming entrenched in the domestic economy.

The index tracks the prices companies charge each other for services such as transport, communications, finance, real estate, advertising and equipment leasing. The BoJ watches it closely for evidence of how far firms are passing rising labour costs on to service prices, a central part of its case that wage growth and inflation are reinforcing each other. A faster pace suggests that pass-through is gathering momentum rather than fading.

The data contrast with the goods side, where producer price inflation slowed to 6.8% in September from 7.6% in August as fuel subsidies eased some raw-material costs. Services prices rising while goods inflation slows suggests domestic, labour-driven pressure is taking over from imported costs as the main driver.

The BoJ concludes a two-day meeting on Friday and is expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25%, after raising it in September, while signalling it is ready to continue lifting borrowing costs as price pressures build. Most economists expect the next hike in December. The key focus is whether the bank’s updated Outlook Report effectively declares that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, a step it has never taken since adopting the goal in 2013.

Today’s acceleration strengthens the case for that declaration and makes it harder for the board members who opposed September’s hike to argue for easier policy.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Moody’s Zandi says a Fed hike this week would be a mistake as 5% yields do the tightening
item.description:
Zandi’s view runs against market pricing for at least one more hike this year, so it’s more a marker for the doves than a market mover. It does sharpen focus on the tension in this week’s Fed decision. Oil is the pivot: crude climbing back toward wartime peaks on Iran tensions lifts inflation and keeps the Fed on its hiking path, while also squeezing real incomes in a way that strengthens Zandi’s growth warning. With 10-year yields near 5% and credit spreads wider, any hawkish surprise from the Fed risks further pressure on rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and leveraged borrowers. A skip with hawkish guidance, as Goldman Sachs expects, would keep December live.

---

---

Zandi’s case is simple: the bond market has already tightened for the Fed, and hiking into an oil shock risks doing the economy’s real damage for it.

Summary:

  • Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi said on X that a Fed rate hike at this week’s meeting would be a mistake
  • He argues rising market rates are already tightening policy, with the 10-year yield near 5%, mortgages above 7% and wider credit spreads
  • He warns hikes cannot fix oil supply shocks tied to Iran, which will lift inflation but erode real wages and spending
  • Moody’s risk matrix flags an AI stock sell-off, a Fed misstep, intensifying wars, trade escalation and financial repression
  • The Fed funds rate is 3.75% to 4.00% after September’s hike, with the FOMC meeting October 27-28
  • Zandi called the September hike a serious mistake; Goldman Sachs expects a skip this week and a December hike

Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi has warned that raising interest rates at this week’s Federal Reserve meeting would be a mistake, arguing that the bond market is already doing the tightening for the central bank and that a policy error now ranks among the growing risks facing the US economy.

Writing on X on Monday, Zandi pointed to the sharp rise in borrowing costs since the Fed’s September hike. The 10-year Treasury yield is hovering around 5%, fixed mortgage rates are above 7% and corporate bond spreads have widened. In his view, that rise in market rates is already restraining the economy, which leaves no need for the Fed to add to it. The FOMC meets on October 27 and 28, with the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00% after September’s quarter-point increase, and markets pricing at least one more hike before year-end.

Oil sits at the centre of his argument. With prices climbing back toward their wartime peaks on tensions with Iran, Zandi said higher energy costs will push up inflation, but warned that rate hikes cannot fix a supply problem. Instead, he argued, higher oil prices will erode real wages and consumer spending, and tightening into that squeeze risks tipping the economy into trouble.

Zandi also pointed to Moody’s risk matrix, which ranks threats to the economy over the next 12 to 18 months by likelihood and potential damage. He said it contains a lot of red, with risks including an AI stock sell-off, a Fed misstep, intensifying wars, trade escalation and financial repression.

The warning is consistent with his earlier stance. Zandi described September’s hike as a serious mistake and warned in late September that higher rates were already damaging the economy. The Fed’s case for tightening rests on inflation that remains well above target, with headline PCE estimated at 3.8% in August and core at 3.4%, alongside price pressure from oil, tariffs and AI investment.

Some on Wall Street expect the Fed to wait this week. Goldman Sachs sees a skip in October followed by a hike in December, which would leave Zandi’s argument as much a test for the December meeting as for this one. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6731 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:

Steady services inflation strengthens the case for the Outlook Report to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached 2%, which would support the yen and short-end JGB yields. The bigger moves are still likely to come from the BoJ’s vote split, Ueda’s press conference and Wednesday’s Fed decision. Oil-driven cost pressure tied to the Iran conflict keeps the wider inflation backdrop firm.

---

Japan’s firms are still passing on service costs at a two-year-high pace, handing the BoJ one more piece of evidence for the 2% declaration markets expect this week.

Summary:

  • Japan’s services producer price index rose 3.7% y/y in September (expected 3.7%, prior 3.7% was revised to 3.5%)
  • That holds the annual pace at its highest in more than two years
  • The index tracks prices companies charge each other for services and is watched for wage pass-through
  • Goods producer price inflation slowed to 6.8% in September from 7.6%
  • The BoJ meets October 29-30 and is expected to hold at 1.25%, with a December hike the consensus call
  • Focus is on whether the Outlook Report effectively declares underlying inflation has reached 2%

Japan’s services producer price index rose 3.7% year on year in September, in line with expectations and matching August’s pace, Bank of Japan data showed on Tuesday. That keeps the annual rate at its highest in more than two years, just days before a BoJ policy meeting where the bank’s assessment of inflation is expected to matter more than the rate decision itself.

The index, also known as the corporate services price index, tracks what companies charge each other for services such as transport, communications, finance, real estate, advertising and equipment leasing. Because these services are labour-intensive, the data are watched as a gauge of whether rising wages are being passed through into prices, a key part of the BoJ’s case that inflation in Japan is becoming self-sustaining.

The steady reading contrasts with the goods side, where producer price inflation slowed to 6.8% in September from 7.6% in August as government fuel subsidies helped ease some raw-material cost pressure. Holding firm against that backdrop suggests domestic service-sector price pressure is proving more durable than the imported cost pressure that drove much of Japan’s earlier inflation.

The release comes ahead of the BoJ’s October 29-30 meeting, where the bank is widely expected to hold its policy rate at 1.25% after raising it in September. Most economists expect the next hike in December. The bigger focus this week is whether the BoJ’s updated Outlook Report effectively declares that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, a step it has never taken since adopting the goal in 2013. Governor Kazuo Ueda said after last week’s G20 meeting that underlying inflation was broadly close to 2% and that the bank could not tolerate a further rise.

Markets will also watch the vote. The two board members who opposed September’s hike could dissent again in favour of a rate cut, a move that would soften the bank’s hawkish message and likely weigh on the yen. Today’s data does little to strengthen their case.

item.title: Greer warns $3.4 billion EU loan to Airbus may breach US-EU aircraft trade truce Alt headlines:
item.description:
This is a warning shot rather than an escalation, so the immediate market impact is likely confined to aerospace names, with Airbus and Boeing shares the most exposed to any shift in trade rhetoric. The bigger risk is that aircraft financing becomes a fresh front in US-EU trade tensions at a time when the administration is already fighting on several fronts, including Canada. Any move toward formal measures, such as reviving tariffs linked to the old subsidy dispute, would weigh on European aerospace and the wider supply chain. A quick EU response with loan details would likely defuse the issue.

--- The Boeing-Airbus feud is back on Washington’s radar, with Greer warning that Europe’s record loan to Airbus could unpick a hard-won aircraft truce unless Brussels starts sharing details.

Summary:

  • US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer warned that a European Investment Bank loan to Airbus may violate the US-EU trade truce
  • The roughly $3.4 billion loan was made in June and is a record, and Greer says his office has received no details despite repeated requests
  • Greer says the issue creates substantial uncertainty for transatlantic aerospace trade and must be resolved quickly to avoid breaching the large civil aircraft agreement
  • Boeing asked the US government in July to press for transparency on the loan
  • The loan came amid speculation Airbus would use it to develop a new aircraft model

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has warned the European Union that a record European Investment Bank loan to Airbus could breach the transatlantic trade truce, including a deal governing how large civil aircraft projects are financed, reopening one of the longest-running flashpoints in US-EU trade relations.

In a statement on Monday, Greer said his office had received no details of the roughly $3.4 billion loan, made in June, despite repeated requests for information. He said the situation was creating considerable uncertainty for transatlantic trade in aerospace, and that it needed to be resolved quickly to keep production in the sector market-driven and to avoid a breach of the large civil aircraft agreement, which he described as hard-won.

The European Investment Bank is the EU’s lending arm, and the loan is the largest of its kind, according to Reuters. It came amid speculation that Airbus would use the money to develop a new aircraft model. US planemaker Boeing asked the US government in July to press for transparency over the financing, setting up the latest round of scrutiny.

Government support for aircraft makers has long been a source of friction between Washington and Brussels, with each side accusing the other of unfairly backing its national champion. The large civil aircraft agreement was designed to set ground rules on that support, so any finding that the loan breaches its terms would put the arrangement, and the broader trade truce it sits within, under strain.

Greer stopped short of announcing any action, instead framing the issue as one that needs urgent resolution. That leaves room for a negotiated outcome if the EU provides the information Washington is seeking. However, the warning adds to a crowded trade agenda for the US administration, which is also locked in tense talks with Canada over tit-for-tat tariffs.

For now, the dispute is a warning shot rather than an escalation. The next steps to watch are whether the EU or the European Investment Bank responds with details of the loan terms, and whether Washington moves from public pressure toward formal measures. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA’s 0.8% forecast
item.description:
The Australian dollar and front-end yields are set up for a binary reaction. With implied hike odds already above half, a trimmed mean at or above 1.0% would push November pricing closer to fully priced and support the currency. A 0.9% or lower print could see that pricing unwind quickly. Oil is central to the headline story: the fuel spike reflects the global energy shock tied to the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would keep headline inflation elevated into year-end. The services component matters most for the RBA, since broadening price pressure would undercut the argument that this is purely an imported energy shock. The release coincides with RBA officials appearing before Senate Estimates, adding to the event risk.

---

---

Australia’s core inflation is set to overshoot the RBA’s own forecast for another quarter, and with the banks split down the middle, Wednesday’s print may decide whether the Board hikes on Melbourne Cup Day.

Summary:

  • Australia’s September quarter CPI is due at 00:30 GMT Wednesday (20:30 US Eastern Tuesday)
  • The big four banks see quarterly trimmed mean inflation at 0.9% to 1.0%, above the RBA’s 0.8% forecast, with headline at 1.2% to 1.3% q/q and 3.9% y/y
  • CBA expects fuel prices up about 10% in September, taking annual fuel inflation to around 24%, and market services inflation rising to 4.3%
  • The cash rate is 4.60% after four hikes this year; the RBA decides on November 3
  • ANZ and Westpac expect a November hike, while CBA and NAB expect a hold, with CBA flagging a growing risk of another move
  • Implied hike odds jumped above 50% after Deputy Governor Hauser said the inflation outlook was materially worse than projected

Australia’s September quarter inflation data, due at 00:30 GMT on Wednesday (20:30 US Eastern on Tuesday), is expected to show underlying price pressure running well ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s own forecast, sharpening the debate over whether the central bank hikes again on November 3. The big four banks broadly expect trimmed mean inflation, the RBA’s preferred core measure, to rise about 1.0% over the quarter, compared with the RBA’s August projection of 0.8%.

Big four forecasts, September quarter CPI (q/q / y/y)

The forecasts are tightly clustered. Westpac is the only bank below 1.0% on the quarterly trimmed mean, while NAB is slightly lower than its peers on headline inflation.

Fuel is the main driver of the headline number. CBA expects fuel prices to rise about 10% in September after an increase of nearly 15% in August, taking annual fuel inflation to roughly 24% as the global energy shock feeds through to the pump. On the monthly measure, CBA sees headline annual inflation climbing to 4.2% in September from 4.0% in August, with the annual trimmed mean steady at 3.6%. The more important signal for policymakers may be services, where CBA expects annual market services inflation to edge up to 4.3% from 4.1%, a sign that price pressure is not confined to energy.

The RBA has already raised the cash rate four times this year, most recently by 25 basis points in September, taking it to 4.60%. Market expectations for a further move rose sharply after Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook was materially worse than the RBA had projected in August, with implied odds of a November hike jumping from about a quarter to more than half.

The banks are split on what the RBA will do. ANZ and Westpac have a November hike as their base case, and ANZ says a 1.0% trimmed mean print would reinforce that view. CBA and NAB expect a hold, though CBA describes the decision as finely balanced and says the risk of another hike is growing, given softer activity, a weaker labour market and subdued consumption on the other side of the ledger.

A trimmed mean at or above 1.0% would strengthen the case for back-to-back hikes, while a reading closer to the RBA’s 0.8% would give the Board room to pause.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac’s Ellis says read the data calls
item.description:
For rates traders, the note argues against reading too much into tone shifts between the press conference and market-focused speeches, and in favour of the minutes and officials’ data interpretations as the cleaner signal. The Governor describing the labour market as a little tight, plus staff’s downbeat view of supply capacity, leans hawkish and supports pricing for further tightening rather than a pause. The coming fortnight is dense with event risk for the Australian dollar and front-end yields: the quarterly CPI lands alongside Senate Estimates testimony, followed by the November decision, the Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches. With supply shocks driving inflation, including energy, a firm CPI would reinforce the hawkish read.

---

---

The RBA has never been chattier, but Westpac’s Luci Ellis says traders hunting for promises should listen instead to how it reads the data, because that is where the real signal lives.

Summary:

  • Westpac Group chief economist Luci Ellis counts 58 RBA public engagements so far this year, matching all of last year and above 52 in 2024
  • Delivery has shifted from set-piece speeches toward fireside chats and broad media interviews, aimed partly at the general public
  • Press conferences target the public, so tone can sound softer than in market-facing forums; Ellis says the minutes better reflect the Board’s view
  • Speeches are more technical, focusing on neutral rates and financial conditions, and a spot check suggests they are harder to read than in 2021
  • The RBA still gives no forward guidance; its interpretation of data, such as the Governor calling the labour market a little tight, is the key signal
  • The run-up to November includes Senate Estimates alongside the quarterly CPI, then the decision, Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches

The Reserve Bank of Australia is talking more often, in more places and on more technical subjects than it did a few years ago, but it still is not promising anything about the path of interest rates, according to Westpac Group chief economist Luci Ellis. In a note on RBA communication, she argues that the clearest signal of future policy lies in how officials interpret incoming data, rather than in any form of forward guidance.

Ellis counts 58 public engagements on the RBA’s speeches page so far this year, already matching the total for all of last year and above the 52 recorded in 2024. Delivery has shifted too, away from set-piece policy speeches toward semi-scripted fireside chats and interviews across a wide range of media, part of a broader effort to explain decisions to the general public at a time when rates are rising but households are not the main source of inflation.

That wider reach can confuse markets, Ellis says, because different audiences call for different tones. The post-meeting press conference is aimed at the public, so a Governor who sounds softer there may simply be acknowledging that policy is causing pain, much as a doctor warns that a treatment might hurt without stopping it. Where tone differs, she argues, pre-drafted material such as the minutes is a more reliable guide to the Board’s thinking than off-the-cuff answers.

The content has also become more technical. Officials increasingly discuss estimates of unobservable variables such as neutral interest rates and financial conditions, and a spot check of readability scores suggests recent speeches are harder to read than those from 2021. The RBA has also stressed that monetary policy works through several channels beyond mortgage repayments, though Ellis notes that if the cashflow channel is the smallest, as the Deputy Governor suggested, a small group of households is bearing a heavy cost for limited effect on inflation.

The practical takeaway is to read the RBA’s interpretation of data. Ellis highlights that the Governor described the labour market as a little tight after the September meeting, even though the Board’s statement did not, and says the Deputy Governor’s recent hawkish tone was no surprise given staff’s downbeat view of supply capacity. With Senate Estimates coinciding with the quarterly CPI release ahead of the November decision, there will be plenty for markets to parse.

The liquidity call is the key one to watch: any signal from the Fed on slowing balance sheet growth further, or on tightening financial conditions, would matter more for his timeline than AI headlines. Wilson says the worst of the correction has already happened beneath the surface, and once AI, the midterms and Fed liquidity clear, the index can catch up with an 8,000 year-end target.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley’s Michael Wilson says the bearish adjustment in US stocks that began in June is entering its final stages, targeting the S&P 500 at 8,000 by year-end
  • Around 60% of Russell 3000 stocks are down more than 20% since the transition began, and 96% of semiconductor stocks have suffered drawdowns that large
  • The tactical downside target stays at 7,100 to 7,200, a slight break of the 200-day moving average
  • Three clearing events: AI capital concerns coming to a head within three to four weeks, the midterm elections, and Fed liquidity, which he calls the most important
  • The S&P 500 has averaged around 17% gains in the 12 months after midterms
  • The sentiment gauge is at neutral and Q3 earnings growth is expected near 27%; Wilson sees buying opportunities ahead

Morgan Stanley’s chief US equity strategist Michael Wilson says the bearish adjustment in US stocks that began in June is entering its final stages, and he has identified three clearing events that he expects to mark a bottom and set up a year-end rally in the S&P 500 to 8,000.

In a note published on Monday, Wilson described the correction as a mid-cycle transition that has done far more damage beneath the surface than the headline index suggests. Around 60% of stocks in the Russell 3000 have fallen more than 20% since the shift began, he wrote, with semiconductors hit hardest: 96% of the sector has suffered drawdowns of that size. Early-cycle groups, including chips, financials, consumer cyclicals and autos, have lagged as investors rotated into higher-quality companies. The S&P 500 itself has held up well, trading around 7,690 at the time of reporting, less than 2% below its record high set early in October. Wilson said breadth has started to improve, suggesting the index and the wider market are converging as the transition is absorbed.

His tactical downside target for the S&P 500 remains 7,100 to 7,200, which would be a slight break below the 200-day moving average, a widely watched gauge of the longer-term trend.

The first of Wilson’s three catalysts is AI. He expects investor concerns over returns on capital, the cost and availability of funding, safety and local opposition to data centre projects to come to a head over the next three to four weeks. The second is the midterm elections, which tend to weigh on stocks beforehand but have historically been followed by strong gains, with the S&P 500 averaging a rise of around 17% in the 12 months after a midterm vote.

The third, which Wilson considers the most important, is liquidity. In his assessment, the Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh has slowed balance sheet growth by roughly half while leaving rates behind the curve with inflation still above target. Financial conditions have tightened sharply, he said, to a degree comparable with 2018 and nearly as severe as the deliberate tightening of 2022.

With Morgan Stanley’s sentiment gauge at neutral and third-quarter earnings growth expected at around 27% year on year, Wilson argues that attractive buying opportunities should emerge as these events resolve over the coming weeks. The view remains a forecast, and a slower resolution of any of the three catalysts would delay the bottom he expects.

The BoJ is set to stand still on rates this week while moving a big step forward on rhetoric, unless two dovish dissenters steal the headlines and the yen pays for it.

Summary:

  • MUFG expects the BoJ to hold at its October 29-30 meeting, with back-to-back hikes considered only in a serious emergency, according to a Nikkei report citing a senior official
  • The updated Outlook Report is likely to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached the 2% target, a new phase for policy normalisation under Ueda
  • After last week’s G20 meeting, Ueda said underlying inflation was broadly close to 2% and that the BoJ could not tolerate a further rise
  • MUFG expects a relatively hawkish tone at Ueda’s post-meeting press conference
  • The key risk: the two board members who opposed September’s hike could dissent against a hold and call for a cut, likely prompting yen selling
  • US Treasury Under Secretary Erin Browne was reported as saying Japan is no longer in deflation and policy should adjust

The Bank of Japan’s policy meeting on October 29 and 30 is unlikely to deliver a rate hike, but it could mark a turning point in how the central bank describes inflation, according to a preview from MUFG. The bank expects the BoJ’s updated Outlook Report to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached the 2% price stability target, which would take the normalisation pursued under Governor Kazuo Ueda into a new phase.

A back-to-back increase looks off the table. MUFG noted a Nikkei report citing a senior BoJ official as saying the bank would consider consecutive hikes only in a serious emergency. MUFG said that could in theory include a sharp rise in USD/JPY following an unexpected rate hike by the Federal Reserve, though it sees that scenario as unlikely. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September.

Ueda has already been laying the groundwork for a firmer message. Speaking after last week’s G20 meeting, he said underlying inflation was now broadly close to 2% and that the BoJ could not tolerate a further rise. That built on his remarks after the September meeting that the policy phase had changed, and reinforced the bank’s sharper focus on containing inflation. MUFG therefore expects the tone of Ueda’s post-meeting press conference to be relatively hawkish.

External pressure points in the same direction. US Treasury Under Secretary for International Affairs Erin Browne was reported over the weekend as saying Japan is no longer in a deflationary environment and that its monetary policy should adjust accordingly.

The main risk MUFG flags comes from inside the board. The two members who voted against the September rate hike could dissent again, this time opposing a hold and instead calling for a rate cut. MUFG said such a move by the BoJ’s reflationist members would reinforce the bank’s dovish image and would likely prompt yen selling, undercutting the hawkish signal from the Outlook Report and Ueda’s press conference.

For markets, the week’s outcome may therefore hinge less on the rate decision than on the vote split and the language around underlying inflation.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda

item.title: ICYMI: Morgan Stanley sees 10%-15% more downside for Chinese offshore stocks before a bottom

Morgan Stanley thinks China’s stock slide has another leg to go before valuations hit their historical floor, though it still sees Beijing’s support making mainland shares the safer place to wait.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley says offshore Chinese shares could fall a further 10%-15% to around eight times 12-month forward earnings, their historical valuation and historical bottom
  • Mainland-listed shares could see a similar de-rating to around 10 to 11 times forward earnings
  • Drivers cited include selling fears linked to a trust tax, pressure on e-commerce, a weakening economy and elevated global volatility
  • The bank says the past two weeks have worsened negative momentum
  • China’s onshore equities are already in a bear market, and the global retreat in AI stocks has added pressure
  • Morgan Stanley still prefers mainland shares, citing government support and greater exposure to AI and innovation companies

Morgan Stanley has warned that Chinese stocks may have further to fall, with offshore shares potentially dropping another 10% to 15% before reaching what the bank sees as a valuation floor, according to a Bloomberg report.

The bank’s strategists said offshore Chinese equities, the shares of Chinese companies listed outside the mainland, chiefly in Hong Kong, could de-rate to around eight times 12-month forward earnings. That level matches their historical valuation and marks the historical bottom for the market. Mainland-listed shares could see a similar de-rating to around 10 to 11 times forward earnings. Forward earnings multiples measure how much investors pay for each unit of expected profit over the next year, so a lower multiple reflects weaker confidence rather than a change in earnings alone.

According to the report, the strategists pointed to a cluster of pressures behind the accelerating correction: concerns about selling linked to a trust tax, strain on e-commerce companies, a weakening domestic economy and heightened volatility in global markets. They added that developments over the past two weeks have made the negative momentum worse.

The backdrop is already difficult. China’s onshore equities are in a bear market, and the global retreat from AI-related stocks has added to the pressure.

Despite the gloomier outlook, Morgan Stanley continues to prefer mainland-listed stocks over their offshore counterparts. The bank cited government support for the onshore market and its greater exposure to companies in AI and innovation-related sectors. That preference suggests the strategists see policy backing as a partial cushion for mainland shares, even as they expect valuations across both markets to compress further.

The call sets out a clear marker for investors. If offshore shares approach eight times forward earnings, Morgan Stanley’s framework would treat that as historically cheap territory. Until then, the combination of selling pressure, weaker growth and fragile global risk appetite argues for caution over trying to call the bottom early.

  • Goldman Sachs says the AI infrastructure buildout will raise inflation in developed markets, with effects varying by region and fading through 2027
  • Memory prices currently add about 19bp to US core PCE; direct pressures elsewhere are around 0.1 point for now
  • Peak boost is put at 50bp for US core PCE and 20bp for US core CPI; non-US developed markets see an average 25bp lift to core inflation into early 2027, possibly up to 33bp
  • Japan is projected at around 0.3 point and the UK at about 0.2 point
  • GDP boost is modest at 0.3% on average across developed markets through 2026, with Australia highest at 0.6%
  • Goldman cites the concentration of data centre input production among Asian exporters as limiting wider spillovers

The global buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure is adding to inflation across developed economies, according to new analysis from Goldman Sachs, which sees the effect peaking at around 50 basis points on US core PCE inflation before fading through 2027. The bank stressed that the impact will vary by region and should prove temporary.

The main channel is direct price pressure from the hardware behind AI. Goldman estimates that memory prices alone are currently adding about 19 basis points to US core PCE, where those components carry a larger weight in the index. Outside the US, direct pressures are smaller for now, at around 0.1 percentage point in most economies, but the bank expects them to build as higher costs pass through to consumer electronics prices, which carry larger weights in non-US inflation baskets than in American measures.

On that basis, Goldman projects that price pressures directly linked to AI will lift year-on-year core inflation in non-US developed markets by about 19 basis points by the first quarter of 2027, compared with a peak boost of 50 basis points for US core PCE and 20 basis points for US core CPI. Taking all effects together, the bank estimates an average lift to core inflation of 25 basis points in non-US developed markets through early 2027, with potential increases of up to 33 basis points relative to long-run trends. Japan stands out at around 0.3 percentage point, with the UK at about 0.2 percentage point.

The indirect effect, through stronger economic activity, looks limited. Goldman estimates the AI buildout will lift GDP across developed markets by a modest 0.3% on average through the end of 2026, with Australia seeing the largest boost at 0.6%, the euro area 0.2% and the UK 0.1%. The bank attributes the small spillover to the concentration of data centre component production among Asian exporters, which keeps much of the economic benefit within a few supply hubs.

The analysis matters because it adds another source of upward price pressure for central banks already dealing with higher energy costs. Goldman’s view that the effect fades as memory price pressures ease suggests policymakers may treat it as a temporary shock, but its timing, peaking into early 2027, overlaps with a period when many are still judging whether inflation is sustainably back near target. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite
item.description:
The Shadow Board result adds to the case for a hike at the October review, although several members still favour a pause, so a hold would not be a shock. A hike paired with a clear signal of a prolonged pause could limit any boost to the New Zealand dollar, while a hold with hawkish guidance would keep year-end hike pricing alive. Oil is the swing factor: members tied much of the inflation risk to fuel prices and the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would strengthen the case for more tightening. The next inflation release is the near-term catalyst for NZ rate pricing.

---

Earlier:

  • Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation

---

Oil and a sliding kiwi have tipped most of NZIER’s Shadow Board toward another RBNZ hike, though the minority wants the central bank to let its earlier tightening do the work.

Summary:

  • A majority of the NZIER Monetary Policy Shadow Board recommends a 25bp OCR increase at the RBNZ’s October Monetary Policy Review, from 2.75% to 3%
  • Members cite renewed energy price pressure and a weaker New Zealand dollar as raising upside inflation risks
  • Several members prefer to hold and let earlier hikes work, pointing to a soft economy and weak labour market
  • Most expect the OCR to rise over the coming year, with year-ahead views ranging from 3% to 4%
  • Some say further tightening should depend on underlying inflation, inflation expectations and the pace of recovery
  • The next Shadow Board release is due on 7 December, ahead of the RBNZ’s Monetary Policy Statement

A majority of the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research’s Monetary Policy Shadow Board has recommended that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise the Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points at its upcoming October Monetary Policy Review, which would take the rate to 3% from 2.75%. The group, which is independent of the central bank, said renewed pressure on global energy prices and a recent fall in the New Zealand dollar have increased the upside risks to inflation enough to justify another increase now.

The board was not unanimous. Several members argued that the RBNZ should give the increases already delivered more time to work through an economy that remains soft, with a cyclically weak labour market. One bank chief economist said there is a case to slow the pace of tightening, noting that while the short-term inflation picture looks more threatening, the medium-term outlook has not shifted, and that business and consumer surveys show no sign yet of second-round price effects.

Those favouring a hike pointed to a combination of pressures. Members cited the rebound in oil prices, a weaker currency, stronger-than-expected growth and core inflation that has stayed elevated, with one arguing that looking through these shocks has not returned inflation sustainably to the RBNZ’s 1% to 3% target band. Another member framed the decision as finely balanced, warning that with the conflict in Iran continuing, fuel-driven price pressures may prove less temporary than hoped.

A further view urged the bank to deliver the move and then signal a prolonged pause, arguing that clarity on the end of the tightening cycle would do more for business confidence than leaving the threat of further increases hanging over the economy.

Looking further out, most members agreed the OCR should rise over the coming year, with views of where it should sit in twelve months ranging between 3% and 4%. Some said the pace of further tightening should depend on how underlying inflation, inflation expectations and the recovery evolve. Several members flagged upcoming inflation data as important, and that release is likely to shape whether the RBNZ moves now or waits until year-end, as many commentators expect.

---

The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) is an independent economic research and consulting organisation based in Wellington, and its Monetary Policy Shadow Board is a panel of economists, academics and business leaders that meets ahead of each Reserve Bank of New Zealand decision. The key distinction is that the board says what the RBNZ should do, not what it will do. Each member assigns percentage weights to the policy options they prefer, and NZIER averages those preferences into a collective view. That makes the result a policy recommendation rather than a forecast or preview of the likely outcome. The two can differ: this month most members favour a hike, even though, as one member noted, many commentators expect the RBNZ to pause until year-end. NZIER says the exercise is also meant to encourage informed debate, show how a board structure might work, and explore how members could use probabilities to express uncertainty. The board is independent of the RBNZ, and members’ views are their own, not those of their employers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Citadel Securities warns AI trade has little margin for error as three risks converge
item.description:
The note gives a framework for the recent equity sell-off: a market priced for AI success has little cushion if returns slip, approvals drag or financing costs keep climbing. Heavy AI capex spenders with thin or negative free cash flow look most exposed, while diversified platforms with established cash flows are better placed. Oil is the wider macro threat, with Brent above $117 and reports of possible renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms keeping energy risk alive. That risk works against any easing from a Fed already facing sticky inflation. Credit is the channel to watch: widening spreads could raise financing costs for leveraged data centre projects even if Treasury yields fall.

---

Earlier:

  • The once Magnificent 7 are not so magnificent, but they still are large cap technology movers

---

Citadel Securities says the AI story has been carrying the market past a pile of other risks, and as faith in that story wavers, those risks become much harder to ignore.

Summary:

  • Citadel Securities says the recent equity sell-off shows investors want firmer evidence that AI spending will produce matching profits, with higher yields adding urgency
  • Meta’s Q3 capex of around $35bn exceeded operating cash flow of about $33bn, leaving free cash flow negative, with roughly $49bn to $59bn more implied for Q4
  • Ramp data show business AI token spending hit a new high in early October, but falling prices mean dollar spending understates usage growth
  • Political risk is rising: a Reuters/Ipsos poll shows 69% of Democrats and 43% of Republicans back limits on data centre construction
  • Pew data show 50% of US adults now see data centres as mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38% in January
  • Brent above $117, fiscal easing and tariffs are raising the cost of financing and running the economy, leaving the Fed in a difficult spot if AI investment slows

Citadel Securities has warned that the AI trade has very little room for error, arguing in a macro note that doubts over returns on the AI buildout are converging with political pushback and a costlier economic backdrop just as the stock market and wider economy have become heavily dependent on the theme.

The note reads the recent sharp equity sell-off as a sign that investors are becoming more demanding about whether extraordinary spending will deliver equally extraordinary profits, with higher bond yields making that question more urgent. Scrutiny now runs across the whole chain, from whether customers achieve real productivity gains, to whether model developers keep pricing power, to whether infrastructure revenues cover financing and depreciation costs. Capex has become a two-sided risk, the note argues: cuts would raise doubts about the investment cycle, while further increases raise questions about financing and eventual returns. Meta is cited as an example, with third-quarter capital spending of around $35 billion exceeding operating cash flow of about $33 billion, leaving free cash flow negative, and full-year guidance implying roughly $49 billion to $59 billion more in the fourth quarter.

Citadel Securities still sees strong demand for AI, pointing to Ramp data showing business token spending reached a new high in early October, though falling prices and efficiency gains mean dollar spending understates usage growth. Cheaper inference benefits customers, but supplier profits depend on how fast costs fall relative to prices. The note continues to favour diversified platforms with established cash flows.

Politics is the second pressure point. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 69% of Democratic voters and 43% of Republicans support limits on data centre construction, while Pew Research Center data show the share of US adults who see data centres as mostly bad for home energy costs rose to 50% in August from 38% in January. The note warns that permitting delays could add interest costs for leveraged projects and leave capacity arriving into a weaker pricing environment, and that AI-linked cyber concerns risk prompting broad restrictions.

The third layer is macro. Fiscal easing and tariffs have raised the cost of financing and operating the economy, while Brent crude trading above $117 a barrel this week adds to the energy squeeze. The note cautions that an AI-led investment slowdown alongside renewed energy disruption would leave the Federal Reserve facing weaker growth and an uncomfortable inflation backdrop, and that widening credit spreads could offset any fall in Treasury yields. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Carney says Canada has not budged as US trade deal looks less imminent than claimed
item.description:
The Canadian dollar had some deal optimism built in after the weekend remarks from Washington, so Carney’s comments and the Semafor report remove part of that support and leave USD/CAD sensitive to further trade headlines. A deal that eases retaliatory tariffs would still be a positive for Canadian exporters and cross-border supply chains, so any concrete breakthrough could still bring a sharp move. For oil, Canada is a major supplier of crude to the US, which keeps energy flows in focus whenever tariff talks shift. With the two governments framing progress so differently, traders are likely to want specifics before pricing a deal again.

---

Earlier:

  • US and Canada working on deal to ease tariffs on Canadian steel and auto imports

---

Washington says a deal is close, Ottawa says it hasn’t moved an inch, and the truth probably sits somewhere in the gap between the two.

Summary:

  • Canadian PM Mark Carney says Canada has not changed its position in trade talks with the US
  • Carney says any progress made is because the US has moved closer to Canada’s position
  • He acknowledged a slight intensification in the negotiations
  • Semafor, citing sources, reports a US-Canada deal is likely not as imminent as US officials indicated
  • On Sunday, NEC Director Kevin Hassett said negotiators were very close to a deal easing tit-for-tat tariffs, a view echoed by President Trump

Hopes for a quick US-Canada trade agreement faded on Monday after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa has not changed its position in talks with Washington, and that any progress made so far reflects the US moving closer to Canada’s stance. The comments came as Semafor, citing sources, reported that a deal is likely not as imminent as US officials had suggested over the weekend.

The pushback follows upbeat remarks on Sunday from Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, who said negotiators were very close to an agreement that would ease the tit-for-tat tariffs between the two countries. US President Donald Trump echoed that optimism.

Carney struck a more guarded tone. He acknowledged a slight intensification in the talks, but framed it on Canada’s terms, saying that to the extent progress has been made, it is because the US has come closer to Ottawa’s position. He also stressed that Canada’s own stance is unchanged, a signal that his government is not preparing to make fresh concessions to get a deal over the line.

Taken together, the two sides are describing the same negotiations very differently. Washington is projecting momentum, while Ottawa is emphasising that any movement has come from the US side. That gap matters because each government has domestic reasons to appear firm, and public claims of being close to a deal can be a negotiating tactic as much as a statement of fact. Semafor’s report adds weight to the view that the remaining differences are more than technical.

None of this rules out an agreement. More intensive talks suggest both sides see value in reaching one, and a deal that eases retaliatory tariffs would reduce costs for businesses on both sides of a deeply integrated border. The near-term question is whether the talks produce a concrete framework or a set of specific tariff reductions, rather than further statements of optimism. Until then, markets are likely to treat claims of an imminent deal with more caution than they did over the weekend. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 26 Oct: Anthropic IPO puts AI back in focus as stocks rebound

AI moved back into the spotlight Monday as Anthropic’s public IPO filing gave traders another reason to assess both the opportunity—and the enormous financing requirements—behind the industry’s expansion.

U.S. stocks moved higher, while oil pulled back. The dollar strengthened against all the major currencies in your closing snapshot, but gold still managed a modest gain. Treasury trading was more divided, with shorter yields rising and longer yields edging lower.

Anthropic: A big IPO—and a big test for AI

Anthropic filed for an IPO, applying to list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. The maker of Claude has taken another step toward becoming a publicly traded company, although the filing leaves the number of shares and offering price unset. Filing for an IPO is a step toward a listing; the shares have not begun trading. sec.gov

InvestingLive reported expectations that the offering could raise more than $100 billion at a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Those remain potential deal parameters, rather than a priced offering. investinglive.com

The growth is substantial. Anthropic reported more than $16 billion in first-half revenue, roughly 14 times the year-earlier amount. That gives investors evidence of rapidly expanding demand, but the company also disclosed substantial losses.

For traders, the question is straightforward: How much is that growth worth, and how much additional capital will be needed to support it? A successful offering would demonstrate continued appetite for AI exposure. It would also bring another major company competing for investor dollars. My takeaway is that enthusiasm for the technology and discipline about valuation will need to travel together.

Dollar finishes higher across the board

The USD gained against every major currency Its largest advance was against the Japanese yen, while its smallest gain was against the Canadian dollar:

Treasury curve flattens

The curve flattened as shorter maturities underperformed. That was consistent with continued caution about the near-term policy outlook, even as longer yields found some relief.

The Treasury also sold $69 billion of 2-year notes at 4.708%, slightly above the 4.705% when-issued yield. That 0.3-basis-point tail indicated buyers required a small yield concession. Investinglive.com

U.S. stocks rebound; chips lead

The closing levels shows:

  • Dow industrial average: 52,297.02, +0.16%.
  • S&P 500: 7,675.07, +0.67%.
  • Nasdaq Composite: 26,186.93, +0.89%.

Semiconductors outperformed, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gaining more than 3%. Tesla rose around 5.3% following a Barclays upgrade. Anthropic’s filing helped put AI back in focus ahead of major technology earnings and the Fed decision.

Chip and AI shares lead the rebound

Chipmakers and companies tied to the AI infrastructure buildout were among the session’s strongest performers. The buying extended beyond processors to optical networking, memory, storage, power generation and cooling equipment.

In your late-session snapshot, the winners included:

  • Lumentum (LITE): +8.19%

Anthropic’s IPO filing put the AI growth story back in the spotlight. The breadth of Monday’s gains suggested buyers were looking across the infrastructure needed to support that growth. Data centers need chips, but they also need faster connections, storage, reliable electricity and cooling.

After last week’s pressure on technology shares, buyers made a stronger showing. The next question is whether earnings and spending guidance can give them a reason to keep going.

European shares finish higher

The European closing snapshot showed broad gains:

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,410.85, +0.91%.
  • France’s CAC 40: 7,847.33, +0.83%.
  • U.K. FTSE 100: 10,767.32, +0.72%.
  • Spain’s IBEX 35: 19,033.29, +0.23%.

Oil retreats, but geopolitical risk remains

WTI futures were near $101.64, down $1.63, or 1.58%, in your snapshot.

InvestingLive’s oil coverage pointed to relief after anticipated U.S. strikes on Iran did not materialize over the weekend. The risk of further attacks nevertheless remained a support for prices. investinglive.com

Lower oil offered some relief for inflation concerns. However, oil above $100 remains a meaningful cost pressure for businesses and consumers.

Gold holds higher; Bitcoin slips

Spot gold traded near $4,012.36, up $16.55, or 0.41%. Gold held higher despite the stronger dollar, with the modest decline in longer Treasury yields providing a somewhat more supportive backdrop. investinglive.com

Silver was nearly unchanged at $53.856, up 0.05%.

Bitcoin traded at $79,811, down $237, or 0.30%. It failed to follow the equity rebound, showing that Monday’s improvement in risk appetite did not extend evenly across markets. investinglive.com

The next test is follow-through. Traders have an improving equity tone and lower oil, but also a stronger dollar and substantial expectations surrounding AI. Earnings, the Fed and the market’s willingness to finance the next stage of the AI buildout remain the key themes.
